quote: I've had foot surgery, so I've been home for about six weeks.
stewart_read: The customer volunteers a health disclosure unprompted while explaining her availability. The rep's next line jumps straight to scheduling logistics with no acknowledgment.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the disclosure as incidental scheduling context rather than a vulnerability moment, which is plausible since she offered it casually inside an availability answer — but the schema treats any such disclosure as a trust gift regardless of how casually it's delivered.
coaching_implication: Coach a one-line acknowledgment reflex ('Sorry to hear that, hope recovery is going well') before pivoting back to logistics — costs three seconds, builds rapport.

quote: And with all the government changes going on, I ain't counting on them at all.
stewart_read: This is a live cost/incentive-skepticism objection. The rep's response references 'new programs' but never flips her skepticism into urgency or curiosity about her specific numbers.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deliberately deferring the incentive conversation to the closer, consistent with setter_scope_discipline — pricing/incentive detail is closer-tier content.
coaching_implication: Even under scope discipline, the rep could create curiosity ('that's exactly why we want to lock in your numbers now before anything changes') rather than a flat acknowledgment — flag as a missed curiosity-creation opportunity, not a scope violation.

quote: is there anyone else on the title of the home with you?
stewart_read: Customer's answer is genuinely tangled (a tax-related co-title situation) and the rep accepts 'I'm the owner' at 02:01 without confirming whether the other person on title needs to be part of the appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: The customer's own explanation ('I'm the owner') may be sufficient self-resolution, making further probing unnecessary since she asserts sole decision authority.
coaching_implication: When a co-owner answer is ambiguous, a quick clarifying question ('so just you on the appointment then?') closes the loop explicitly rather than assuming from her muddled explanation — protects against a surprise co-owner at the door tomorrow.

quote: All I needed was a quote. You have to come out and measure or something?
stewart_read: The customer's question reveals she booked expecting something different (a remote quote) than what's actually scheduled (an in-person visit). This is a real, unresolved expectation gap at the moment of booking, not just a procedural skip.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's brief clarification ('we just prefer to come by and show you everything') may have been sufficient in the moment since the customer replies 'Oh, okay' and proceeds to book without further pushback.
coaching_implication: Flag for the manager: when a customer's own words show a quote-only expectation, take an extra sentence to sell the value of the in-person visit tied to her stated interest, not just correct the factual record.

quote: Thank you. And and may I get your name, please? May I get your name, please?
stewart_read: The customer asking for the rep's name again at the very end, after he introduced himself as Carter seven minutes earlier, signals the intro didn't land as a memorable anchor and the close was procedurally thin on personalization.
alternative_hypothesis: This could simply be a distracted customer detail unrelated to rep performance, since she was mid-multitasking through much of the call (long pauses, self-corrections on dates).
coaching_implication: Low-cost fix: rep could restate his name once more at the button-up recap ('Alright Jennifer, this is Carter, I've got you down for...') to reinforce the anchor before the close.

quote: And and you're gonna be here or or somebody else is coming by?
stewart_read: This is the second and final instance of the same expectation-setting gap first seen at 06:14 — she still isn't sure what tomorrow's appointment actually looks like or who's attending, right up to the end of the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep answers factually and she accepts it ('Nope. That's fine.'), so on its face the exchange resolves cleanly.
coaching_implication: Two separate moments of the same confusion by call's end is a pattern, not a one-off — worth naming to the rep as a signal the button-up recap needs to spell out who is coming and why, not just when.

quote: Hey. This is Carter calling from ION.
stewart_read: Rep states name and company but doesn't reference the form submission until the next breath at 00:13; a minor stylistic gap rather than a legitimacy risk, since the customer shows zero suspicion anywhere on the call.
alternative_hypothesis: None needed — the customer's cooperative, unguarded tone throughout confirms this was never read as suspicious by her.
coaching_implication: Low priority: combining the form reference into the same breath as the intro would tighten the open, but this is a polish note, not a fix for a real problem on this call.
